projects.title: Which Employers Reliably Sponsor H-1B Business Roles
projects.hook: SQL analysis of 3.47M H-1B filings (2020–2023). The business-role wage premium survives on medians — then breaks honestly when IT managers are excluded.
projects.visualAlt: Wage premium by year, business vs data roles

body.problem: International graduates pick a track first and ask about visa risk later — on anecdote. Nobody could say whether business and analytics tracks differ on approval odds, or which employers sponsor every year rather than once.
body.approach: Normalized 3.47M federal filings into a five-table MySQL database, then ran eight queries on volume, approval, pay, and four-year employer durability.
body.hers: Reported the median that broke my own headline finding — the premium flips when IT managers are excluded.
body.result: Approval gap never passed 1.7 points. Business volume +9.1% while analytics fell 6.1%. 77 durable business sponsors identified — EY leads with 13,329 filings at 97.8%.
body.lesson: Visa risk is the wrong variable. The decision turns on market direction and pay, not approval odds.

projects.title: Massachusetts H-1B Analysis
projects.hook: Reading the Massachusetts labor market through five years of public H-1B filing data: which employers sponsor repeatedly, and do business roles pay as well as analytics roles?
projects.visualAlt: Median pay: business roles vs data-and-analytics roles
projects.diagramAlt: Trap, Insight, Machine: the build-post framework

body.problem: I'm on an F-1 visa. The job search isn't just finding the right role — it's finding an employer who'll go the full distance: OPT to STEM OPT to H-1B. I needed to know whether the business roles I'd apply to get sponsored as often, and pay as well, as the data-and-analytics roles.
body.approach: Filtered 137,866 Massachusetts H-1B filings (FY2020-2024) to 123,497 certified, normalized every wage to annual, grouped roles by federal occupation code instead of keywords, and compared business vs analytics with bootstrap confidence intervals on the medians.
body.hers: Caught 2,583 IT managers hiding in the business group through their occupation code — they'd inflated the business median to $115,000. Re-ran without them: $105,000. The notebook shows exactly what changed.
body.result: 13,672 business filings vs 14,035 analytics. $105,000 vs $104,000 median pay — statistically the same. 0% vs 100% STEM — the H-1B clock is tighter on the business side.
body.lesson: Pay doesn't decide the track — the visa clock does. Same money, different runway.

projects.setting: Solo. Python, pandas, matplotlib — one notebook, 22 cells, reproducible end to end.
projects.context: International graduates choose between business and analytics roles partly on which gets sponsored — and whether the pay justifies the track.
projects.outcome: Business roles pay effectively the same as analytics roles: $105,000 vs $104,000 median. The difference is the visa clock — 0% STEM vs 100% STEM.

projects.title: Where Should We Spend the Next Ad Dollar?
projects.hook:
A marketing analytics lead has an ad budget and a room full of managers who
read the business through sales volume. This dashboard makes the case for
spending it elsewhere — and lets the room test the recommendation live.

Built in Tableau for Hult's Data Visualization course (QTM-6032R). Graded
100/100. What it demonstrates: turning analysis into a decision a room
can act on — the bridge between the technical work and the business language. Live on Tableau Public
· Interactive dashboard

body.problem:
As marketing analytics lead, defend an ad budget to management.
Management reads the business through sales volume and wants the sub-category
picture across the USA. Dataset: 9,994 order lines, 17 sub-categories,
49 states, 2016–2019.
body.approach:
Four linked views — sales bar, sales-vs-profit scatter, discount
ladder, state map — driven by four interactions: a filter action, a hover
highlight, a Profit Target parameter with reference line, and a type-ahead
highlighter. A Discount Ceiling what-if slider was prototyped after submission
(see methodology). A five-point Tableau Story walks the argument: what sells → selling ≠ earning → the discount cause →
the map proof → Fund / Fix / Stop. Colour rule throughout: blue = profit,
orange = loss, readable for red-green colour blindness.
body.result:
The recommendation: fund Paper (43%), Copiers (37%),
Accessories (25%), Labels (44%), Envelopes (42%); fix pricing first on
Binders, Storage, Chairs; stop funding Tables, Bookcases, Machines,
Supplies. Capping discounts at 20% lifts profit 47% on its own.

calls:
Trap: Budget follows sales volume. Phones sells $330K, Chairs $328K, Tables
is #4 — so the money goes to the biggest sellers, including one that loses
$17,725.

Insight: The discount ceiling. No discount level above 20% makes money:
at or below 20% the business earns +$422K; above 20% it loses −$135K. The
states confirm it independently — average discount and margin correlate at
r = −0.98.

Machine: The ceiling as a testable number. The analysis verifies it two
ways — the discount ladder (+$422K at or below 20%, −$135K above) and the
state map (r = −0.98) — and a Discount Ceiling slider prototyped after
submission lets a reader perform the cap instead of taking the number on
trust. The live workbook ships four interactions: filter, highlight, Profit
Target, highlighter.

projects.title: Delivery Economics
projects.hook: A white-glove delivery operation losing $1,156 on 13 orders — and the fix isn't routing, it's pricing. I rebuilt the whole case from 171 raw order lines: the cost model, the 7-day operating schedule, and the operating system that runs the day. The presentation, the dashboard, the operations design, and every number below are reproducible from the raw data.

body.problem: I was asked to optimize the operation: routes, truck loading, and the daily schedule for 13 Bay Area customers. I built the cost model from 171 raw order lines, optimized down to 7 days and 21 truckloads, and proved the loss is structural — then rebuilt the whole thing for publication with case-accurate numbers.
body.approach: Objective: minimize total operational cost subject to the service promise — not distance (it only touches 8% of cost), not utilization (100% would split customer orders across days). Sequence: geographic clustering, bin-pack to the 1,700 cu ft truck without splitting orders, assign to days inside the 540-minute window. Solver demoted to a ceiling test after it returned disconnected loops. Three alternatives tested: two trucks (+$1,092, rejected), luxury pace (+$3,040 — the price tag of the promise at its extreme), bigger truck (−$1,664, the only lever that wins).
body.result:
$6,043 cost vs $4,887 revenue: −$1,156, −23.7% margin. Eight of thirteen customers lose money; the five smallest subsidize the rest. Recommendations: volume-based pricing at $150 + $0.25/cu ft (or +$88.94 per delivery on flat fees), the concierge rescheduling policy for no-shows, and the bigger truck as the capital lever — it flips the loss into a $508 profit.

Full write-up: CASE-STUDY.md.

projects.context: Four sources, all in data/: 171 order lines, a 45-SKU item master (volume/weight per piece), customer addresses for zone mapping, and the case-documented operating parameters. analysis/recompute.py reproduces every number on this page from those files — run it.
calls: All 171 lines mapped with zero misses. Volume binds before weight. Three customers drive 41% of the volume. And the audit caught three contradictions in my own original files — a crew rate missing the driver premium, a mileage figure that didn't feed the fuel math, a scenario verdict contradicting its own numbers. All fixed from the primary sources; the loss moved from $808 to $1,156 and the thesis held.
